title: Job 18:11–21
context: Bildad continues his poem on the fate of the wicked: terror, disease, death personified as “the king of terrors,” a ruined dwelling, no descendants, and no remembered name, ending, “This is the place of him who doesn’t know God” (18:21). Several images appear to echo Job’s own losses, so the poem functions as an implied accusation. The book does not endorse that application (42:7).

verses.text: Terrors will make him afraid on every side, and will chase him at his heels.
verses.arminianNotes: “Terrors will make him afraid on every side, and will chase him at his heels.” Arminian readers see the inner dread Bildad assigns to the wicked, drawn in vivid poetic language.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the poem moving from outward traps to inner fear. Readers in this tradition note that Job does experience terror, which may be why Bildad’s words wound so deeply.

verses.text: His strength will be famished. Calamity will be ready at his side.
verses.arminianNotes: “His strength will be famished. Calamity will be ready at his side.” Arminian readers see Bildad describing exhaustion and looming disaster as the lot of the wicked.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the poem’s steady accumulation of misfortune. Bildad presents it as certain, while the wider book shows that calamity can come upon the righteous as well.

verses.text: The members of his body will be devoured. The firstborn of death will devour his members.
verses.arminianNotes: “The firstborn of death will devour his members.” Arminian readers see a grim figure for deadly disease, and many hear an allusion to Job’s own illness, though the phrase’s exact sense is uncertain.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise treat the phrase “firstborn of death” as a poetic figure, probably for a fatal disease. Readers in this tradition note that Bildad seems to describe Job’s condition while calling it the wicked man’s fate.

verses.text: He will be rooted out of the security of his tent. He will be brought to the king of terrors.
verses.arminianNotes: “He will be brought to the king of terrors.” Arminian readers commonly take the phrase as a personification of death, ending the wicked man’s security in his tent.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see death personified. Some readers compare ancient Near Eastern imagery of death as a ruler, though such comparisons are suggestive rather than certain.

verses.text: There will dwell in his tent that which is none of his. Sulfur will be scattered on his habitation.
verses.arminianNotes: “Sulfur will be scattered on his habitation.” Arminian readers see an image of a dwelling left desolate, and some hear an echo of the judgment on the cities of Genesis 19:24.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a picture of devastation. The possible echo of Genesis 19 is suggested by some readers, but Bildad’s point is simply that nothing of the wicked man’s home will remain.

verses.text: His roots will be dried up beneath. His branch will be cut off above.
verses.arminianNotes: “His roots will be dried up beneath. His branch will be cut off above.” Arminian readers see the image of a withered tree, describing the loss of both life and descendants.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see a tree cut off root and branch. Readers in this tradition note the painful resonance with Job’s loss of his children, which Bildad seems to take as evidence against him.

verses.text: His memory will perish from the earth. He will have no name in the street.
verses.arminianNotes: “His memory will perish from the earth. He will have no name in the street.” Arminian readers see the loss of remembrance, a deep fear in the ancient world.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the threat of being forgotten. Ironically, Job’s own words and name are preserved in Scripture, which some readers see as part of the book’s answer to Bildad.

verses.text: He will be driven from light into darkness, and chased out of the world.
verses.arminianNotes: “He will be driven from light into darkness, and chased out of the world.” Arminian readers see Bildad’s picture of total expulsion from life and community.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the climax of the wicked man’s ruin. Readers in this tradition remember that Bildad describes a fate he assumes, not one the narrator has assigned to Job.

verses.text: He will have neither son nor grandson among his people, nor any remaining where he lived.
verses.arminianNotes: “He will have neither son nor grandson among his people.” Arminian readers see a cutting line in light of Job’s bereavement, and they read it with sorrow at how the friend’s theory wounds.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise feel the harshness of this line given Job’s loss of his children in chapter 1. They see it as a warning against applying general truths to sufferers without compassion.

verses.text: Those who come after will be astonished at his day, as those who went before were frightened.
verses.arminianNotes: “Those who come after will be astonished at his day.” Arminian readers see Bildad claiming that the fall of the wicked becomes a public example to later generations.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the wicked man’s ruin presented as a spectacle. Readers in this tradition note that people do later marvel at Job, but in the book’s ending it is his restoration that is remembered.

verses.text: Surely such are the dwellings of the unrighteous. This is the place of him who doesn’t know God.”
verses.arminianNotes: Bildad concludes, “This is the place of him who doesn’t know God.” Arminian readers see the implied charge against Job, which the book later answers in the LORD’s rebuke of the friends (42:7).
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the summary verdict Bildad wants Job to accept. Readers in this tradition stress that the book does not endorse this application, and 42:7 judges the friends’ words about God.
